name: The Cell Nucleus (1831)
teaser: Robert Brown, the botanist who also discovered Brownian motion, was studying orchids when he noticed a dark spot inside every cell — the nucleus. It was the first hint that cells have a command center, and it gave biology its word for the brain of the cell.

exploreAction.targetName: Brown's 1831 observations on the orchid family
exploreAction.instruction: Brown described the 'areola' or nucleus in a footnote to a botanical paper — he had no idea how important it was. Read how the nucleus was later shown to hold chromosomes and DNA, making it the seat of heredity. Two centuries on, 'nucleus' still names the cell's information center.

name: Mitosis Described (1879)
teaser: Walther Flemming stained salamander cells and watched, for the first time, the choreography of cell division: chromosomes doubling, lining up, and pulling apart into two new nuclei. He called it mitosis, from the Greek for thread — and it is the process behind every growth in your body.

exploreAction.targetName: Flemming's 1882 book 'Zellsubstanz, Kern und Zelltheilung'
exploreAction.instruction: Flemming couldn't watch live cells, so he fixed and stained them at different stages and assembled a time-lapse from stills. Read how his drawings — still recognizable today — revealed that chromosomes split lengthwise and are shared equally between daughter cells. He coined the word 'chromatin.'

name: The Neuron Doctrine (1888)
teaser: Santiago Ramón y Cajal, using a silver stain that marks single cells, saw that the brain is built of separate, individual neurons that touch but never merge — information flows one way along each cell. The idea that neurons are distinct cells, the neuron doctrine, is the foundation of all neuroscience.

exploreAction.targetName: Cajal's Golgi-stain drawings and 1888 papers
exploreAction.instruction: Cajal improved Camillo Golgi's stain and used it on young brains, where neurons are sparser and clearer. Read how his exquisite drawings of the cerebellum revealed the one-way flow of signals and the tiny gaps — synapses — between cells. He and Golgi shared the 1906 Nobel, though they disagreed to the end.

name: The Sodium–Potassium Pump (1957)
teaser: Every cell in your body spends a third of its energy pumping sodium out and potassium in — a molecular machine that keeps nerves able to fire and muscles able to contract. Jens Christian Skou, a young Danish scientist working alone in his lab, discovered it in a crab nerve, and won the 1997 Nobel.

exploreAction.targetName: Skou's 1957 paper on the Na+/K+-ATPase
exploreAction.instruction: Skou found an enzyme in crab leg nerves that splits ATP only when sodium and potassium are both present — the molecular pump. Read how he initially couldn't get funding or attention, and how the discovery became the prototype for all ion pumps, transporters, and channels. It explains how the heart drug digitalis works.

name: The Action Potential (1939)
teaser: Alan Hodgkin and Andrew Huxley pushed a fine glass electrode inside a giant squid nerve fiber and measured the electrical spike of a nerve impulse as it passed — the first recording from inside a nerve cell. Their model of the action potential won the 1963 Nobel and still underlies neuroscience.

exploreAction.targetName: Hodgkin & Huxley's 1939 intracellular recording from the squid giant axon
exploreAction.instruction: The squid's giant axon — a millimeter thick — was the only nerve big enough for their electrode. Read how they measured the impulse overshooting zero, proving the membrane's permeability to sodium briefly reverses, and how their four-equation model of channels predicted everything. It is one of the great quantitative feats of biology.

name: Lysosomes Discovered (1955)
teaser: Christian de Duve, fractionating rat liver cells in a centrifuge, kept finding a digestive enzyme leaking from broken particles — a 'suicide bag' he named the lysosome. These little sacs of acid and enzymes are the cell's recycling and waste-disposal system, and their failure causes storage diseases.

exploreAction.targetName: de Duve's 1955 identification of lysosomes
exploreAction.instruction: The enzyme acid phosphatase appeared in the soluble fraction only after the particles had been damaged — de Duve realized a fragile organelle was breaking open. Read how this accidental pattern revealed the lysosome, how it digests worn-out parts and invaders, and how de Duve shared the 1974 Nobel.

name: The First Tumor Virus (1911)
teaser: Peyton Rous ground up a chicken sarcoma, filtered it through a porcelain filter fine enough to trap all cells, and injected the clear liquid into healthy chickens — which grew tumors. Cancer could be transmitted by something smaller than a cell: the first tumor virus, later named Rous sarcoma virus.

exploreAction.targetName: Rous's 1911 papers on a transmissible avian sarcoma
exploreAction.instruction: Rous's result was met with decades of skepticism — cancer was thought to be a disorder of the cell itself. Read how the discovery was vindicated when the virus's gene, v-src, was found to be a hijacked copy of a normal cell gene, proving some cancers are born from our own growth switches. Rous won the 1966 Nobel, 55 years late.

name: The First Oncogene (1976)
teaser: Harold Varmus and Michael Bishop asked a radical question: is the cancer gene in Rous's virus actually a normal gene that the virus stole from cells? They proved yes — the first oncogene, a growth switch that every animal carries and that causes cancer when it misfires. The discovery rewrote our picture of cancer.

exploreAction.targetName: Stehelin, Varmus, Bishop & Varmus's 1976 paper on cellular src
exploreAction.instruction: The team showed that normal chicken DNA contains a gene nearly identical to the virus's transforming gene, v-src — so the virus stole a cell's own growth gene and turned it against it. Read how this single idea — cancer genes are normal genes gone wrong — opened the door to molecular oncology and won the 1989 Nobel.

name: The p53 Tumor Suppressor (1979)
teaser: A protein called p53 was found in abundance in cancer cells — but instead of causing cancer, it turned out to be the cell's guardian: a protein that halts division, repairs DNA, or orders a damaged cell to die. More than half of all human cancers carry broken p53. It is the most studied protein in cancer biology.

exploreAction.targetName: The discovery of p53 (1979) and its later identification as a tumor suppressor
exploreAction.instruction: p53 was first misread as an oncogene because it accumulates in tumors — later understood as a broken guardian piling up uselessly. Read how David Lane and others cloned it, how the 'guardian of the genome' concept emerged, and why restoring p53 is a dream of cancer therapy. It's named for its molecular weight, 53 kilodaltons.

name: The Taung Child (1924)
teaser: A fossilized skull of a three-year-old, part ape and part human, arrived in Raymond Dart's lab in South Africa packed in a box labeled as a gift. He chipped it free from rock with his wife's knitting needles and announced a new species: Australopithecus africanus — the first early human ancestor found in Africa.

exploreAction.targetName: Dart's 1925 Nature paper on Australopithecus africanus
exploreAction.instruction: The child had a small ape-sized brain but human-like teeth and an upright posture — the foramen magnum, where the spine enters the skull, sat underneath, as in walkers. Read how the scientific world mocked Dart for decades, and how the discovery of more australopiths proved him right. Africa was the cradle, after all.

name: Peking Man (1929)
teaser: At a cave near Beijing, workers under Davidson Black and then Pei Wenzhong pulled out skulls of Homo erectus half a million years old — and, astonishingly, layers of ash suggesting they may have used fire. The original fossils vanished during World War II; casts and photographs survive.

exploreAction.targetName: The Zhoukoudian excavations and the 1929 Peking Man skull
exploreAction.instruction: Pei Wenzhong found the first complete skullcap on December 2, 1929, working by candlelight. Read how the fossils — lost in 1941 while being shipped to America — are known today only from casts, and how Peking Man's heavy brow and brain size confirmed the human family's deep roots in Asia as well as Africa.

name: The Neanderthal Fossils (1856)
teaser: Quarry workers in the Neander Valley in Germany blasted out a skeleton with a heavy brow and a sloping skull. Johann Carl Fuhlrott, a local teacher, recognized it as something unprecedented — a fossil human. Named Neanderthal man, it was the first ancient human relative ever recognized.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1856 discovery and Fuhlrott's 1857 description of the Neanderthal remains
exploreAction.instruction: The workers nearly threw the bones away as a bear's; Fuhlrott and anatomist Hermann Schaaffhausen argued they were a primitive human. Read how Darwin's Origin of Species, published three years later, gave the discovery its meaning — and how Neanderthals went from 'degenerate human' to a distinct species to, today, our cousins who live on in our DNA.

name: Turkana Boy (1984)
teaser: Kamoya Kimeu, Richard Leakey's fossil hunter, spotted a bone fragment eroding from a slope in Kenya that led to the most complete early human skeleton ever found — a Homo erectus boy, 1.6 million years old, already nearly as tall as a modern human. It showed our ancestors became tall and fast long before they got big brains.

exploreAction.targetName: The 1984 discovery of the Nariokotome skeleton (KNM-WT 15000)
exploreAction.instruction: The skeleton lacks only hands and feet, making it the reference point for early human anatomy. Read how his height — about 5'3" as a child of eight or nine, headed for 6 feet — proved that Homo erectus bodies were built for long-distance walking in open country, long before the brain's expansion. A new species of ape-man, discovered by accident.

name: Ardi (1994)
teaser: In Ethiopia's Afar desert, Tim White's team found the skeleton of Ardipithecus ramidus, 4.4 million years old — a million years older than Lucy, and nearly as far back as our split from chimpanzees. Ardi walked upright in the forest, and her anatomy redrew the picture of our earliest steps.

exploreAction.targetName: The 2009 publication of Ardipithecus ramidus ('Ardi')
exploreAction.instruction: The skeleton was crushed so flat it took 17 years to reconstruct — White's team worked out each bone in 3D. Read how Ardi's pelvis shows upright walking combined with grasping feet, suggesting our ancestors walked before they left the trees. Ardi toppled the idea that bipedalism came from savanna living.

name: The Dmanisi Skulls (1991)
teaser: In the Republic of Georgia, excavators beneath a medieval town found five skulls of early Homo, 1.8 million years old — the oldest human fossils found outside Africa. Small-brained and varied, they suggest that one variable species walked out of Africa, not a perfected one.

exploreAction.targetName: The Dmanisi hominin discoveries (1991–present)
exploreAction.instruction: The skulls — plus stone tools and animal bones with cut marks — show our genus left Africa soon after it evolved. Read how one skull's small brain and large face made researchers question how many early Homo species really existed, and how Dmanisi reshaped the story of the first exit from Africa.

name: Troy Excavated (1871)
teaser: Heinrich Schliemann, a German businessman who had made a fortune and retired to find Homer's Troy, dug a huge trench into a Turkish hill and struck ancient city after ancient city, stacked like layers of a cake. He had found — or believed he had — the city of the Iliad.

exploreAction.targetName: Schliemann's excavations at Hisarlik (1871–73)
exploreAction.instruction: Schliemann dug through nine cities, blasting through the upper levels to reach what he thought was Homer's Troy. Read how he found 'Priam's Treasure' — gold he may have smuggled out of Turkey — and how modern archaeology shows the site was indeed a wealthy Bronze Age citadel matching the Iliad's geography, destroyed by fire around 1180 BCE.

name: Mohenjo-daro (1922)
teaser: A Buddhist stupa mound in the Indus Valley hid one of the world's first cities — Mohenjo-daro, 'mound of the dead,' with grid streets, covered drains, and water tanks, built 4,500 years ago. It revealed the Indus Valley Civilization, a peer of Egypt and Sumer that wrote in a script still undeciphered.

exploreAction.targetName: The discovery and excavation of Mohenjo-daro (1920s)
exploreAction.instruction: Banerji found a carved seal beneath the stupa; his supervisor John Marshall soon realized the scale. Read how the city's baked-brick architecture, sophisticated sanitation, and the great bath showed an advanced urban order, and how the mystery of the unread script still keeps the civilization's voice silent.

name: Machu Picchu Revealed (1911)
teaser: Hiram Bingham, an American explorer hunting for the last Inca capital, followed a local farmer up a jungle ridge and walked into a lost city of terraces and temples perched between two peaks. He called it the 'lost city of the Incas' — actually a royal estate built around 1450 and abandoned a century later.

exploreAction.targetName: Bingham's 1911 expedition to Machu Picchu
exploreAction.instruction: The city was never truly 'lost' — locals knew it — but Bingham made it world-famous. Read how his expedition found intact temples, the Intihuatana solar stone, and hundreds of structures, and how Machu Picchu's mountaintop siting and dry-stone masonry still leave engineers guessing. It is now Peru's most-visited ruin.

name: The Nazca Lines (1927)
teaser: From the air, Peru's desert floor is covered with giant figures — a hummingbird 300 feet long, a spider, a monkey, and hundreds of straight lines. First noted by archaeologists in 1927 and publicized from planes in the 1930s, they were made by the Nazca people by scraping away dark stones to expose pale earth, 2,000 years ago.

exploreAction.targetName: The discovery and study of the Nazca geoglyphs
exploreAction.instruction: The figures are invisible from the ground — which is why they were only fully mapped from the air. Read how the Nazca created them with simple tools and how they may have been walked as ceremonial paths for rain rituals. The straight lines stretch for miles, aligned with nothing; their purpose is still debated.

name: The Palace of Knossos (1900)
teaser: Arthur Evans, an English archaeologist, bought a hill in Crete and uncovered a vast labyrinthine palace of 1,300 rooms with running water and a throne still in place — the center of the Minoan civilization, Europe's first great culture, which he named for the legendary King Minos.

exploreAction.targetName: Evans's excavations at Knossos (1900–1930s)
exploreAction.instruction: Evans found frescoes of leaping bulls, storage jars taller than a person, and clay tablets in two scripts he named Linear A and Linear B. Read how his 'reconstruction' of the palace in concrete is now criticized, and how Linear B was finally deciphered in 1952 to reveal — surprisingly — an early form of Greek.
